title: Step 10 - Restart the Game
section: 20. Boss Level Challenge 2 - The Simon Game
summary: Final step of the Simon build: write a startOver() function that puts the game's state variables back to their starting values, and call it when the player presses a wrong button so a key press can begin a fresh game.

concepts.heading: Game state that must be reset
points: Three global variables control a run of the game: level (the current round number), gamePattern (the array of colours the computer has chosen so far) and started (a boolean flag that says whether a game is in progress).
Resetting means assigning each one its initial value again: level = 0, gamePattern = [], started = false.
userClickedPattern does not need resetting here because nextSequence() already empties it at the start of every round.

concepts.heading: Why these three values restart the game (Extra)
points: (Extra) The keydown handler only starts a game when started is false (if (!started) {...}). While started stays true after a loss, key presses are ignored, so the game cannot restart. Setting it back to false re-arms that handler.
(Extra) level must go back to 0 because nextSequence() increments it before displaying it; starting from 0 makes the first round of the new game show 'Level 1'.
(Extra) gamePattern must be a new empty array; otherwise the new game would continue appending to the old sequence and the player would have to repeat the previous game's colours.
(Extra) Putting the reset in its own named function keeps checkAnswer() readable: the else branch handles the game-over feedback (sound, red flash, title text) and then hands off to startOver().

concepts.heading: Where to call it
points: Call startOver() inside the else branch of checkAnswer(), i.e. the branch that runs when the colour just clicked does not match gamePattern at the same index.
(Extra) Call it after the game-over feedback code from Step 9, so the title change to 'Game Over, Press Any Key to Restart' is already set when the state is wiped.

task.name: Simon Step 10: restart the game
task.starting_point: game.js from Step 9: the game detects a wrong answer, plays wrong.mp3, flashes the body with the game-over class and changes the h1 to 'Game Over, Press Any Key to Restart', but pressing a key does nothing because the state is never reset.
task.goal: After a game over, pressing any key starts a brand-new game at Level 1 with a fresh random sequence.
steps: Declare a new function named startOver() in game.js.
In its body, set level back to 0, set gamePattern to an empty array, and set started back to false.
Inside checkAnswer(), in the else branch that handles a wrong click, add a call to startOver() after the game-over code.
Test: play until you make a mistake, see the game-over message, press a key and confirm the title shows Level 1 and only one button flashes.
task.expected_result: The game loops indefinitely: lose, press any key, and a new game begins from Level 1 with no leftover colours from the previous sequence.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 20 - Boss Level Challenge 2 - The Simon Game/script.js

pitfalls: Forgetting to reset started: the keydown listener's if (!started) guard then blocks every restart attempt.
Resetting level to 1 instead of 0, which makes the restarted game open on Level 2 because nextSequence() adds one first.
Defining startOver() but never calling it from the wrong-answer branch.
Declaring level, gamePattern or started with var inside startOver(); that creates new local variables and leaves the globals unchanged.

gaps_and_ideas: Blurb for a new lesson 'Simon step 10: reset state': a game is just a few variables; restarting means putting them back the way they started.

Task 1: write startOver() that resets level, gamePattern and started. Task 2: call it in the wrong-answer branch. Task 3: predict what happens if started is left true, then try it. Task 4: explain why level resets to 0 and not 1.
Starter code: a stripped-down Simon with the four coloured divs, keydown starter, nextSequence() and checkAnswer() already written, with a TODO where startOver() goes.
Interactive demo: a live 'state panel' beside the board showing level, gamePattern, userClickedPattern and started updating on every click and key press, so learners watch the reset happen.
